A member of the [[New Zealand Labour Party|Labour Party]], she was first elected to Parliament in 2008 for a three-year term as a [[List MP|list Member of Parliament (MP)]], and was re-elected as MP for [[Kelston (New Zealand electorate)|Kelston]] in 2014. In 2023, she was elected as the [[Deputy Leader of the New Zealand Labour Party|deputy leader of the Labour Party]], succeeding [[Kelvin Davis (politician)|Kelvin Davis]]. Sepuloni is New Zealand's first MP of [[Tongan New Zealanders|Tongan descent]].{{cite news |date=23 January 2023 |title=Carmel Sepuloni makes history as first Pasifika deputy PM |publisher=[[Radio New Zealand]] |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/morningreport/audio/2018874642/carmel-sepuloni-makes-history-as-first-pasifika-deputy-pm |quote=Carmel Sepuloni was New Zealand's first MP of Tongan descent}} She was a senior minister in the [[Sixth Labour Government of New Zealand|Sixth Labour Government]] under [[Prime Minister of New Zealand|Prime Minister]] [[Jacinda Ardern]], holding office as [[Minister for Social Development (New Zealand)|Minister for Social Development]] throughout the government's term, and additionally serving as Minister for Arts, Culture, and Heritage, [[Minister for ACC]], [[Minister for Workplace Relations and Safety]], [[Minister for Disability Issues]], and [[Minister for Pacific Peoples]]. She became deputy prime minister in January 2023, when the Labour leadership switched to [[Chris Hipkins]].{{Cite web |title=Live: 'Biggest responsibility of my life' – Hipkins confirmed as PM |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/chris-hipkins-sworn-in-as-prime-minister-carmel-sepuloni-as-deputy-jacinda-ardern-vacates-top-job/IERZGZV2BFAE5AWLNJHMMGHYQ4/ |access-date=24 January 2023 |website=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |language=en-NZ}} ==Early years== Sepuloni was born and raised in [[Waitara, New Zealand|Waitara]], [[Taranaki]], and attended [[New Plymouth Girls' High School]].{{cite web |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/131030608/who-is-the-new-deputy-prime-minister-carmel-sepuloni |title=Who is the new Deputy Prime Minister Carmel Sepuloni? |date=22 January 2023 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] }} Her father was a [[Samoans|Samoan]]-[[Demographics of Tonga|Tongan]] migrant [[Meat-packing industry|freezing worker]], who migrated to New Zealand without being able to speak English, and "staunch [[Trade union|unionist]]" and her mother was a [[Pākehā]] from a conservative farming family. She moved to Auckland in 1996 to attend the [[Auckland College of Education]] and [[University of Auckland]] where she attained a Diploma of Teaching (Primary) and a Bachelor of Education, respectively. She also holds a Postgraduate Diploma in Education. Sepuloni worked as a teacher in [[Samoa]] and in alternative education programmes in Auckland. Later, she worked as an equity manager and a research project manager in Pacific health at the University of Auckland.{{cite news |date=22 January 2023 |title=Who is new Deputy Prime Minister Carmel Sepuloni? |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/131030608/who-is-new-deputy-prime-minister-carmel-sepuloni |access-date=23 January 2023 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |language=en}}{{cite web |title=Hon Carmel Sepuloni |url=https://www.beehive.govt.nz/minister/biography/carmel-sepuloni |access-date=23 January 2023 |website=beehive.govt.nz |publisher=New Zealand Government |language=en}} She has two sons.{{Cite web |date=23 January 2023 |title=Who is Carmel Sepuloni? New Zealand's first Pasifika deputy prime minister |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2023/jan/23/who-is-carmel-sepuloni-new-zealand-first-pasifika-pacific-deputy-pm-prime-minister |access-date=23 = 54th |start = {{NZ election link year|2023}} |end = present |electorate = Kelston |party = New Zealand Labour Party |list = 3 }} {{End}} ===First term, 2008–2011=== Sepuloni came to Parliament in the [[2008 New Zealand general election|2008 general election]] having successfully stood as a list-only candidate for the [[New Zealand Labour Party]]. She had been involved in the party for only a year and a half before being elected. Sepuloni's position at 35th on the party list, and the promotion of other new candidates, was cited by ''[[The New Zealand Herald]]'' as an effort by the Labour Party to "inject new faces" and increase the party's ethnic diversity.{{cite news |url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10529963 |title=New generation to fly party flag at election |first1=Audrey |last1=Young |first2=Paula |last2=Oliver |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=1 September 2008 |access-date=10 September 2009 |archive-date=23 May 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110523105726/http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10529963 |url-status=live }} After the election, Sepuloni became Labour's spokesperson for [[Ministry of Civil Defence & Emergency Management (New Zealand)|civil defence]] and associate spokesperson for tertiary education and social development.{{Cite news|url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz-election-2008/news/article.cfm?c_id=1501799&objectid=10541851&pnum=0|title=The back bench baby MPs|first=Alice|last=Neville|date=9 November 2008|access-date=2 October 2012|work=[[The New Zealand Herald]]|archive-date=19 October 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121019172349/http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz-election-2008/news/article.cfm?c_id=1501799&objectid=10541851&pnum=0|url-status=live}} In her [[maiden speech]], Sepuloni said, "I've learned through my own experiences and the experiences of others around me, that our young in particular can quickly begin to self-stigmatise when the media and society stigmatise them. When the media only portrays a picture of a ghettoised, poverty-stricken group of trouble makers, then our youth can resign themselves to the fact that this is what they are. They may even take pride in this prescribed image, because it provides them with a level of attention and status which although negative, is attention and status nonetheless." In June 2010, Sepuloni's Employment Relations (Probationary Period Repeal) Amendment Bill was drawn from the member's ballot. A bill to repeal the changes to probationary employment contained in the [[Employment Relations Amendment Act 2008]],{{cite web |url=http://www.parliament.nz/en-NZ/PB/Legislation/Bills/e/e/2/00DBHOH_BILL10016_1-Employment-Relations-Probationary-Period-Repeal.htm |title=Employment Relations (Probationary Period Repeal) Amendment Bill |publisher=Parliament of New Zealand |access-date=18 June 2010 |archive-date=19 August 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100819060126/http://www.parliament.nz/en-NZ/PB/Legislation/Bills/e/e/2/00DBHOH_BILL10016_1-Employment-Relations-Probationary-Period-Repeal.htm |url-status=live }} it was defeated at its first reading 64 votes to 57.{{cite web|url=http://business.scoop.co.nz/2010/08/05/member%E2%80%99s-bill-to-remove-90-days-voted-down/ |title=Member's Bill to remove 90 day probationary period voted down |publisher=New Zealand Labour Party |date=5 August 2010 |access-date=10 August 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110723132208/http://business.scoop.co.nz/2010/08/05/member%E2%80%99s-bill-to-remove-90-days-voted-down/ |archive-date=23 July 2011 }} === 2011 election loss === On 19 March 2010, Sepuloni was selected as the Labour candidate for the [[Waitakere (New Zealand electorate)|Waitakere electorate]] in the [[2011 New Zealand general election|2011 general election]], facing incumbent National MP and Cabinet minister [[Paula Bennett]]. In April 2011, she was ranked number 24 on the party's list for the election. On the election night preliminary count, she placed second in Waitakere, 349 votes behind Bennett, and with her list ranking was set not to be returned to Parliament. When the official results were released on 10 December 2011, Sepuloni had received sufficient [[special vote]]s to win Waitakere and defeat Bennett by eleven votes.{{cite web |url= |url-status=live }} === Government minister, 2017–2023 === During the [[2017 New Zealand general election|2017 general election]], Sepuloni stood again in her Kelston seat, returning to Parliament with a majority of 16,789 votes. Following Labour's formation of a [[Sixth Labour Government of New Zealand|coalition government]] with [[New Zealand First]] and the [[Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand|Greens]],{{cite web|url=http://www.radionz.co.nz/news/political/342022/video-who-s-in-who-s-out|access-date=20 October 2017|title=Who's in? She was subsequently appointed as [[Ministry of Social Development (New Zealand)|minister of social development]] and disability issues as well as associate minister for Pacific Peoples, and [[Minister for Arts, Culture and Heritage|arts, culture & heritage]].{{cite web |title=Hon Carmel Sepuloni |url=https://www.parliament.nz/en/mps-and-electorates/members-of-parliament/sepuloni-carmel/
